Understanding the practice effect on motor learning using a web-based platform

PI: Yue Du, PhD This is a study examining how we learn motor skills
Contact
Yue Du
  • Thincmolab_online@tamu.edu

Overview

Participants will learn and practice to respond to sets of visual stimuli (e.g., numbers, letters of English alphabet, letters of the Phoenicial alphabet, a hand image representing spatially-matched cues with participant’s responding hand, geometrical shapes, spatial locations, and/or fractals) by pushing corresponding buttons on a keyboard. 

Participants will be required to perform this task under self-paced manner, and under time pressure conditions cued by external visual/auditory signals.

Inclusion criteria (all must be met):

  • Ability to give informed consent and understand the task
  • Over the age of 18 years and under 65 years of age
  • English-speaking
  • Participants must self-report:
    • Have no known neurological disease (e.g., Stroke, Parkinson Disease, Apraxia etc.).
    • Have no difficulty typing on a keyboard.

Duration

One-session study lasting about 2 hours

Compensation

Up to $30 
Paid as Amazon gift card

Location

Online Only

title.rendered: Interactions of gallotannins with the intestinal microbiome

content.rendered:
1. Home
  2. Aggie Research Volunteers
  3. Interactions of gallotannins with the intestinal microbiome

Interactions of gallotannins with the intestinal microbiome

PI: Susanne Talcott, Ph.D  The objective of this study is to evaluate the impact of tannase-treatment of gallotannins via sumac tea on the intestinal microbiome, absorption of metabolites and cognitive function in a 6-week randomized, placebo controlled cross-over double-blinded nutritional intervention study in healthy adults. 
Contact
Elizabeth Culpepper
  • sumacstudy@gmail.com

Overview

Three participant groups will be asked to consume 12 oz of sumac tea daily, with or without the addition of tannase, for 6 weeks with the addition of a probiotic or placebo capsule. The main procedures in the study include: blood draws, stool collection, urine collection, digital cognitive function assessments (CANTAB), anthropometrics (body weight, height, body fat percentage, BMI) and vitals (temperature, blood pressure, and heart rate) along with health history questions.  

You are invited to take part in this research study because you are between the ages of 18-65 years old and have not had any of the following conditions with or without hospitalization and/or drug treatment within the last 6 months: acute cardiac event, seizures, stroke, cancer, liver or renal dysfunction, pregnancy or lactation, hepatitis B or C, HIV, inflammatory bowel disease, or celiac disease.  

Duration

Approximately 6 weeks

Compensation

$400.00

Location

Bryan-College Station – on-campus

IRB Approval Date: 08/08/2025

Aperiodic Slope and MRI

PI: Rebecca Brooker, PhD We leverage team expertise in developmental science, a novel aperiodic slope measure, and overlapping neuroimaging techniques to demonstrate and validate aperiodic slope as a usable proxy for neural maturation across a critical period of neurodevelopment.
Contact
PI: Rebecca Brooker, PhD
  • rebeccabrooker@tamu.edu

Overview

This project is being used to develop a novel metric of neurodevelopment, demonstrating its links to psychological constructs that support healthy emotional development during childhood.  Children and 1 parent will participate in two laboratory visits, each lasting approximately 60 minutes. Children will complete an MRI scan, EEG record, short survey, and several behavioral games. Parents will complete a short survey and a behavioral game with their child. 

Inclusion Criteria:

  1. Children have a parent or legal guardian who can provide written consent for participation.
  2. Children were full term (at least 5lbs 8 oz) at birth.
  3. Children are able to provide verbal assent for participation.
  4. Children have no known developmental delays.
  5. Parents and children are able to speak English. 
  6. Parents are able to read English.
  7. Children have no known neurological conditions.
  8. Children have none of the following contraindications for MRI:
    1. metal implanted in the body
    2. implanted medical devices, including braces (determined and verified by the MRI technician)
    3. hearing impairment
    4. Claustrophobia
    5. the inability to lay comfortably on the scanner bed for roughly 20 minutes

Exclusion criteria: 

Failure to meet inclusion criteria.

Duration

2 hours (in the form of two 1-hour visits)

Compensation

$50 per laboratory visit; $10 for parent questionnaires; $10 for child questionnaires

Location

Bryan-College Station – on-campus

title.rendered: Psychometric Properties of a Brief Value Driven Attention Task

content.rendered:
1. Home
  2. Aggie Research Volunteers
  3. Psychometric Properties of a Brief Value Driven Attention Task

Psychometric Properties of a Brief Value Driven Attention Task

PI: Brian Anderson, PhD Co-I – Steven Woltering, PhD The current study investigates the psychometric properties of a brief attention assessment using eye-tracking technology.  
Contact
Jacob Brooks
  • jtbrooks@tamu.edu

Overview

The primary purpose of this study is to investigate the psychometric properties of a brief attention assessment using eye tracking task. At times, previously reward-associated or otherwise motivationally significant stimuli are difficult to ignore even when a person knows that they are irrelevant to the current task, reflecting an involuntary attentional bias acquired through learning. This influence of reward on attention is typically measured using an hour-long assessment, and the present study tests whether it is possible to reliably measure this influence using a much quicker assessment. A secondary purpose of the study is to investigate whether this attentional bias is related to behaviors in everyday life assessed via questionnaire and to reward’s influence on memory.

To be eligible, participants must be: 

  1. Age 18-35 (inclusive)
  2. English speaking
  3. Have normal or corrected-to-normal (e.g., glasses, contacts) visual acuity
  4. Have normal color vision
  5. Must not be allergic to any of the ingredients in M&Ms (including sugar, milk, cocoa, peanut, hazelnut, and almond). Note that the M&Ms used do not contain peanut, hazelnut, and almond as ingredients but are processed in a factory that uses such ingredients, and so are also included as potential allergens.
  6. Must not have anything to eat for at least 3 hours leading up to the experiment. 

Duration

55 minutes across two lab visits (35 minutes for visit 1; 20 minutes for visit 2). 

Compensation

Up to $20: Participants are compensated $5 per lab visit in the form of a gift card. Each participant will have an opportunity to earn an additional $5 during each lab visit for task-related reward. 

Location

Bryan-College Station – on-campus

title.rendered: The causal links between frontal-limbic brain networks and reward-guided cognitive flexibility

content.rendered:
1. Home
  2. Aggie Research Volunteers
  3. The causal links between frontal-limbic brain networks and reward-guided cognitive flexibility

The causal links between frontal-limbic brain networks and reward-guided cognitive flexibility

PI: Joseph M. Orr PhD To determine how the brain uses rewards to guide flexible behavior and decisions.
Contact
Beatrice Lomeo
  • tamu.congalab@gmail.com

Overview

If you agree to participate, you will be asked to provide a complete set of questionnaires, undergo a brain scan and noninvasive brain stimulation, and complete tasks (much like computer games) at the brain imaging scanner. The study will consist of three separate visits, each about 1 week apart. In the first session you will complete questionnaires, undergo an MRI scan, complete one session of non-invasive brain stimulation, and complete a short computerized cognitive test. The first session of stimulation will determine the signal threshold for the remaining sessions. In the next two sessions, you will undergo a short stimulation procedure and then complete computerized cognitive tasks.

Participants in this study will be right-handed English-speaking adults between the ages of 18 and 30. Participants must be able to safely undergo MRI; participants should not have any of the following: implants (metallic or powered), claustrophobia, large tattoos within the last 6 months, surgery within the last 6 months, non-removable piercings, or permanent makeup, and should be able to lay on their back for up to 30 minutes. Participants will be excluded based on safety measures for non-invasive brain stimulation procedures. This may include a history of seizure, stroke, or neurological disorder, pregnancy, use of stimulant medications, or the presence of metal or magnetic objects near the head. Participants must refrain from alcohol within 24 hours of each session. Additionally, participants must have no self-reported history of allergies to soy, milk, wheat, or nuts, as these allergens are present in the candy provided. All participants will complete a safety screening form prior enrollment in the study.

Duration

3 visits, 5 hours total

Compensation

$20/ hr

Location

Bryan-College Station – on-campus

IRB Approval Date: 02/20/2026

title.rendered: Evaluating changes in brain functional networks during menopause

content.rendered:
1. Home
  2. Aggie Research Volunteers
  3. Evaluating changes in brain functional networks during menopause

Evaluating changes in brain functional networks during menopause

PI: Jessica Bernard, PhD This work is seeking to understand how the hormonal changes and fluctuations of perimenopause impact how brain networks are organized, and in turn how hormone therapy may impact these networks and their changes. We are using a technique called dense sampling with brain imaging, where we will take a lot of measurements (24) over time, in a sample of 8 dedicated women, to better understand how this dynamic time of change impacts the brain in middle-aged and older women.
Contact
Jessica Bernard
  • 979-845-2581
  • Jessica.bernard@tamu.edu

Overview

During perimenopause levels of hormones such as estrogen are fluctuating in the body, and this can lead to cognitive dysfunction, including brain fog, which impacts women’s quality of life. The brain relies on large-scale networks – connections among brain areas – to support cognition. Despite growing evidence suggesting estrogen’s role in brain network organization, research on how hormonal fluctuations impact brain connectivity during menopause is limited. Additionally, hormone therapy (HT) remains controversial, with uncertainty about the optimal timing for its initiation to preserve brain health and prevent neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s. This project aims to explore how estrogen fluctuations during menopause impact brain network connectivity and to evaluate the effects of HT on these changes.

Using resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI), a type of brain imaging where participants relax and let their mind wander, we will examine the impact of menopause and HT on the dynamic functional connections in the brain. This study will use dense-sampling approaches (many longitudinal measures on small samples, in this case, 24 measures across 6 months) to investigate fluctuations in brain network connectivity in humans at different menopausal stages (perimenopause and post-menopause), with and without HT. All participants will undergo weekly brain imaging scans scheduled at the participant’s convenience, provide saliva samples at each visit to measure hormones, answer questionnaires related to menopausal symptoms and health, and wear an Oura ring to track sleep, heart rate, body temperature, and movement. Only females will be included in this study, and participation is limited to 4 participants: 2 perimenopausal participants, and 2 post-menopausal participants. One participant in each category will be using HT and the other will not. There are no strict age limits or exclusions, but we expect that all participants will be over the age of 40. Exclusion criteria include left-handedness and any factor that is a contraindication for the brain imaging environment. 

Duration

Participants will complete 24 visits. These visits will be once per week over the course of 6 months. 

Compensation

Participants will be compensated $20 per visit. They will also receive a completion bonus of $500 for completing all visits, totally $1000. Finally, participants will be asked to wear an Oura ring for the 6-months of the study. After the study is complete they will be able to keep the ring.

Location

Bryan-College Station – on-campus

IRB Info

IRB Number: STUDY2025-0632
IRB Approval Date: 06/26/2025
